query: For HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy, earlier studies separately examined tensile creep at 1250 °C, microhardness changes during cold rolling, elastic moduli from 293 to 1100 K, and hardening after aging at 600–800 °C. However, these findings do not provide a unified explanation of the alloy’s stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior. Thermal expansion is also relevant because mismatch can produce thermal stresses during composite solidification and potentially affect strength. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the unresolved behavior? Specify a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, observations predicted relative to a baseline, the relevant temperature and response boundaries, how the earlier findings support the hypothesis, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The unusual stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior of the HfNbTaTiZr refractory high‐entropy alloy is governed by internal residual stresses that develop from a thermal expansion mismatch between the intrinsically distorted solid‐solution matrix and nanoscale compositional fluctuations or incipient precipitates. These mismatch‐induced stresses alter dislocation mobility (by enhancing solute drag or providing extra pinning) and modify elastic moduli, thereby unifying the disparate observations from tensile creep, cold‐rolling hardening, and temperature‐dependent elastic measurements.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐cast HfNbTaTiZr with a single-phase BCC structure exhibiting inherent lattice distortions and subtle chemical inhomogeneities that may promote nanoscale regions with slightly varying thermal expansion.
generation.intervention: Prepare two sets of samples from the same alloy composition but with controlled thermal treatment: one set is slow cooled (or annealed with a controlled cooling rate) to accentuate thermal expansion mismatch and allow internal residual stresses to develop, and the other is rapidly quenched to minimize such mismatch. All other processing (e.g., cold rolling and aging) is kept constant.
generation.conditions: Perform high‐temperature tensile creep tests and in situ elastic modulus and thermal expansion measurements over a temperature range from room temperature (≈293 K) up to around 1250 °C (≈1523 K) under controlled atmospheres to avoid excessive oxidation. Mechanical loading conditions and strain rate should be maintained constant between the two sample sets.
generation.structural_mediator: Internal residual stress fields arising from differential thermal expansion between the matrix and any nanoscale compositional/precipitate variations.
generation.mechanism: As the temperature increases, the intrinsic lattice distortion of the multi‐principal element matrix causes regions with slightly different thermal expansion coefficients. Their mismatch creates internal stresses that hinder dislocation movement (through an enhanced solute drag or pinning effect) and modify the thermoelastic response—increasing high‐temperature yield strength and creating an anomalous elastic response. In contrast, minimizing the mismatch via rapid quenching lowers these internal stresses, resulting in a more typical temperature dependence of mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the quenched (baseline) state, samples processed to accentuate the thermal expansion mismatch (slow cooled) are predicted to exhibit (1) higher tensile yield strength and lower creep rates at high temperatures; (2) altered elastic modulus behavior when measured from 293 to about 1100 K; and (3) possibly greater hardening upon aging due to an interplay between precipitate stability and the internal residual stresses.
generation.baseline: HfNbTaTiZr processed with rapid quenching to produce minimal internal thermal expansion mismatch and residual stresses.
generation.boundary: Temperature regime from ≈293 K up to ≈1250 °C with mechanical responses (creep, elastic moduli, and hardening) evaluated within these boundaries.
generation.uncertainty: The relative contributions of thermal expansion mismatch versus other mechanisms (such as oxidation effects or purely precipitation‐induced hardening) to the overall strength and elastic behavior are not yet quantitatively known.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two groups of HfNbTaTiZr samples from the same melt alloy: one group is subjected to slow cooling (or a controlled annealing–cooling cycle) designed to enhance thermal expansion mismatch and the resulting internal stresses, while the other is rapidly quenched to minimize such effects. Test both groups under identical high‐temperature tensile creep and in situ elastic modulus measurements across 293 K to 1250 °C.
measurements: Tensile yield strength and creep rate at elevated temperatures (especially near 1250 °C)
Thermal expansion coefficients and elastic moduli (via, e.g., resonant ultrasound spectroscopy or in situ neutron diffraction)
Microstructural characterization (e.g., TEM, XRD) to verify any differences in nanoscale strain fields or precipitation stability
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the slow-cooled samples do not show a statistically significant increase in high-temperature strength (i.e., lower creep rates and higher yield strength) and a measurable difference in elastic modulus or thermal expansion behavior relative to the rapidly quenched samples, then the hypothesis that thermal expansion mismatch–induced internal stresses govern the anomalous behavior is falsified.

Investigations of mechanical properties and microstructure of different MEAs derived from the HfNbTaTiZr alloy system has been performed. It has been shown that ductility is significantly reduced by simultaneous presence of Ta and Zr in the alloy, which leads to reduction of the BCC1 phase content. These elements segregate during solidifying. Because of the miscibility gap in the Ta-Zr equilibrium phase diagram two BCC phases are found after cooling to room temperature. Clear correlation between the BCC1 phase content and the total elongation to failure of the alloy was found. Precipitation of Ta rich precipitates on grain boundaries reduces the elongation to almost zero values. No correlation was found between the tensile mechanical properties and microstructure related parameters in investigated set of alloys. The 5 element HEA alloy exhibits the best combination of strength and elongation. 4 and 3 element MEAs have lower strength to various extent. Some of them are ductile (NbTaTiZr, NbTaTi, NbTiZr) but some of them are brittle (TaTiZr, Nb1.5TaTiZr0.5, Nb0.5TaTiZr1.5) depending on microstructure.
